newsitem.title: FRANCE: France-Soir daily flouts law, publishes six polls.
newsitem.headline: France-Soir daily flouts law, publishes six polls.

text.p: Popular newspaper France-Soir on Saturday followed a lead set by other French dailies by flouting laws banning the publication of opinion polls in the week ahead of elections.

On an inside page on the eve of Sunday's parliamentary election runoff, the newspaper printed six surveys carried out over the past week and available on the Internet computer network or on the French Minitel phone-computer system.
Together with the dailies Le Parisien and the southwest regional newspaper La Republique des Pyrenees, France-Soir runs the risk of a 500,000 franc ($88,000) fine.
On Friday Le Parisien printed results of a poll conducted by a Swiss daily. La Republique des Pyrenees published a poll on May 23 just before the election's first round.

"Why not supply to a curious public all the surveys, including their tiny variations which reveal the fever which has at last seized electors?" France-Soir editor Bernard Morrot wrote in a front-page column.
Dismissing the law as imbecile and outdated, Morrot invoked the republican right to equality given the fact that such surveys are common knowledge among the Paris establishment.

Jean-Marcel Bouguereau, editor of La Republique des Pyrenees wrote that confidential polls were available to people like politicians, stock brokers and journalists and there was no reason the general public should not also have access to them.
The anti-surveys law is meant to avoid swaying voters. The polls, or rumours of them, are a major factor moving the Paris stock market ahead of the election.
Polls taken before the first round all gave the ruling centre-right at least a narrow lead over the left. All were wrong, as the left came out well ahead.
Similar bans apply in Belgium, Spain and Italy. Britain, Germany and the United States have no restrictions on polls.
